answers.children: Yes — Briards are good with children when raised with them, thanks to their loyal and protective instincts that lead them to guard youngsters as they once did livestock on French plains. Their large size and herding background mean they may gently nip at heels to keep children together, while their intelligence helps them read family moods and offer a gentle nudge with their shaggy head. (PawLabs child-friendly score: 7/10)
answers.other-pets: Briards can get along with other pets if introduced early, though their protective herding nature and wariness can create tension with unfamiliar animals as they once guarded flocks from intruders. Their loyalty bonds them tightly to family dogs yet their history of standing against wolves means same-sex aggression sometimes appears when space feels threatened.
answers.exercise: Briards need one to two hours of daily exercise such as long hikes across varied terrain or yard patrols that match their steady farm-dog stamina. Without this their intelligent minds grow restless and they may chew through doorframes in frustration, echoing the purposeful work they were bred for herding and guarding livestock across French countryside.
answers.shedding: Yes — Briards shed moderately with a long double coat that is wavy and thick, causing loose hair to tangle into mats especially around the ears and behind the legs. This shaggy French herding coat traps debris from fields, demanding regular attention to stop it spreading across the house.
answers.hypoallergenic: No breed is hypoallergenic and the Briard is not one commonly suggested for allergy sufferers because its long double coat sheds and produces dander. The thick, wavy texture that protected it while guarding livestock in France continues to release hair and proteins indoors.
answers.training: Briards are trainable for the right owner because their high intelligence and loyalty make them responsive to consistent guidance that channels their protective herding instincts. Their original role defending sheep from wolves without constant direction can lead to independent decisions, so firm patience is required to prevent overprotectiveness toward strangers.
answers.lifespan: Briards live 10-12 years. Their large powerful build developed for centuries of rugged work herding and guarding on French plains supports this span when given purpose and space to move, matching the robust yet not extreme frame that once carried them through long days on the land.
answers.size: Adult Briards weigh 55-100 lb and stand 22-27 in tall at the shoulder. This substantial French herding frame feels imposing indoors yet their shaggy coat softens the impression, while the muscular legs built for patrolling wide pastures make them a solid presence that fills a room and leans affectionately against family members.
answers.barking: Briards bark moderately, most often with a deep rumbling warning when they sense strangers or threats, reflecting their long history as guardians of livestock against wolves and poachers. Their protective loyalty keeps them alert rather than noisy without cause, using their voice to defend the family they bond to so tightly.
answers.apartment: No — Briards do not suit apartment living because their protective instincts and steady energy require space to patrol and exercise or they become restless, while their deep warning bark can disturb neighbours. The breed's need for mental tasks drawn from French herding work adds to the challenge indoors.
answers.first-time: No — Briards are not a good first dog because their high grooming needs from the long thick coat and their wariness of strangers demand experienced handling to prevent overprotectiveness. Their intelligence and deep loyalty reward owners who understand the firm guidance required for a dog bred to guard livestock independently.
